topic: Snap mousetrap: what holds the loaded spring back? A thin locking bar over the jaw, its tip under a tiny lip (catch) on the hinged trigger; a touch tilts the catch and the jaw snaps over
title: What Holds a Mousetrap Back? 🪤
principle: When a snap trap is set, the coiled spring pushes the jaw to swing over; a locking bar hinged at the rear of the base passes over the jaw and holds it back, and the bar's front tip sits under the rearward shoulder (lip) of a catch on the hinged trigger, and because the jaw presses on the bar close to its hinge while the catch holds the far tip, the bar acts as a lever and only a small part of the spring's push reaches the tip (torques balance: l_i F_i = l_o F_o), so the slightest press on the trigger tilts the catch, the lip slides off the tip and the spring swings the jaw over.

firstComment:
Answer: a thin bar on a tiny lip 🔧

When the trap is set, the coiled spring is always trying to swing the jaw over. A thin locking bar passes over the jaw and holds it back. The front tip of that bar sits under a tiny lip on the catch of the hinged trigger, where the bait goes.

Why can a tiny lip hold that strong spring? The bar is a lever. The jaw pushes on it close to its hinge, and the catch holds it far away at the tip, so only a small fraction of the push reaches the tip (a lever balances when force x distance from the hinge is the same on both sides).

The slightest press on the trigger tilts the catch, the lip slides off the bar's tip, and the spring swings the jaw over fast and with great force.

(Simplified 3D model, shown in slow motion. The exact catch shape is different from brand to brand.)

Sources:
W. C. Hooker, US Patent 528,671, Animal-Trap (1894) (the jaw is held back against the spring by a locking-bar which passes over the jaw, hinged at the rear of the base; its front end engages a catch on a hinged trigger, bent rearward to form a shoulder; the slightest pressure on the trigger springs the trap): https://patents.google.com/patent/US528671A/en
Wikipedia, Mousetrap (the spring-loaded bar trap was first patented by William C. Hooker in 1894; the bar swings down rapidly and with great force when anything touches the trip): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mousetrap
OpenStax College Physics 2e, 9.5 Simple Machines (for a lever, l_i F_i = l_o F_o: forces times their distances from the pivot balance): https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/9-5-simple-machines
altText: 3D animation of a wooden snap mousetrap, without voice. A set trap with a coiled steel spring, a wire jaw pulled back, a thin locking bar and a small piece of cheese on a metal trigger, under the question What holds it back? A red circle marks the spot where the bar's tip meets the trigger. 1, the spring pushes the jaw: an orange arrow shows the jaw trying to swing over. 2, the bar holds the jaw down: an arrow presses down where the locking bar crosses the jaw. 3, the bar is a long lever: a big arrow pushes up near the bar's hinge and only a small arrow reaches its far tip. 4, its tip hooks under a lip: a close-up from the side shows the bar tip tucked under a small lip on the trigger's catch. 5, a touch tilts the lip off: a pencil eraser slowly presses the cheese, the trigger tilts, an arrow shows the lip sliding off the bar tip, the tip pops up and, in slow motion, the jaw swings over, SNAP!, and pins the pencil. The payoff reads A tiny lip holds the spring. A follow line appears and the set trap fades back in for the loop.
